Workspaces
Overview
Copy page

Bring your people, apps, and context together in one place to build and run the systems your team relies on.

A workspace is the project container for a Zite build. When you create a new app, form, or database, Zite provisions a workspace so the related pieces can live together.
Every workspace includes one database. You can then add as many apps and forms as the project needs, all connected to the same underlying data.
​
What a workspace includes
Workspaces keep the operational parts of a project in one place.
One database
Each workspace has one Zite Database for the records, tables, and relationships that power the project.
Multiple apps
Add internal apps for your team and external apps for public pages, portals, or other shared experiences.
Forms
Add forms when you need to collect submissions, requests, files, approvals, or updates into the workspace database.
Users & roles
Add editors, manage the people who use each app, and configure database roles.
​
Find things in your workspace
On the workspace overview, press ⌘K to search. Results stay in that workspace by default. Clear the search field to look across your organization. Search is not available inside the app editor.
You can find apps, forms, and tables (not individual rows), plus people, roles, and connections (shown as Integrations). Search also includes Go to and Create shortcuts.
If you have use-only access, search shows published apps. Tables, people, roles, and integrations need editor access.
​
Add apps and forms
A workspace can grow over time. Start with the app, form, or database you need first, then add more apps and forms as the workflow becomes clearer.
Apps can be:
Internal: admin dashboards, team tools, review queues, operations panels, and other apps used by people inside your organization.
External: public-facing apps, landing pages, client portals, partner portals, or other shared experiences that people outside your internal team can launch by link.
Because each workspace has one database, the apps and forms in that workspace can work around the same records instead of becoming separate projects.
​
When to create another workspace
Use a new workspace when the project needs a separate database, a different team of editors, or a separate business system. Keep apps and forms in the same workspace when they should share data and be managed by the same team.
Common reasons to keep work in one workspace:
An internal dashboard and public portal should use the same customer records
A form should create or update records used by an app
The same editors need to manage the database and apps
Several apps represent different views of the same operation
Common reasons to create a separate workspace:
The new project needs its own database
A different team should manage editors, app members, and roles
The apps and forms do not need to share records
The project belongs to a different client, department, or business process

Related topics

How to Build
Create an app
Copy page

Learn how to create a Zite app in a new workspace, import data, match your brand, connect integrations, and write an effective starting prompt.

Zite is best for internal tools, business apps, dashboards, portals, and workflows tied to existing data. It is not the best primary stack for launching a full SaaS product, though you can build external apps and add login when needed. Learn more in What can I build?.
​
Before you build
Creating an app starts a new workspace for that app. If you want to add another app to an existing workspace, open that workspace first and create the app from the workspace homepage.
When Zite provisions a new workspace, it also creates a Zite Database for that workspace. You do not have to use that database in the app, although it’s highly recommended. It is there when you need a shared place to store records, power forms, or connect multiple apps around the same data.
From the create screen, you can also prepare the app before sending your first prompt:
Import data
Bring in existing data from Airtable, CSV, Google Sheets, or Excel before Zite builds the app.
Match brand
Apply a Brand Kit so the first version uses your logo, colors, typography, and brand guidelines.
Integrate
Connect services such as Google Sheets, Airtable, Slack, OpenAI, Email, Notion, and any other integration your app should use.
​
Getting started
1
Choose App
Start from App so Zite builds the user-facing experience in a new workspace. This is the right starting point for dashboards, portals, admin tools, approval queues, onboarding guides, and other business apps.
2
Optional: Import data when needed
Use Import data to bring in Airtable, CSV, Google Sheets, or Excel data before building. This helps Zite understand the records and fields your app should work with from the start.
3
Optional: Match your brand
Use Match brand to apply a Brand Kit before building so Zite can match your logo, colors, fonts, and guidelines. You can also create a new Brand Kit at this stage, or choose and change a theme later.
4
Optional: Connect integrations
Use Integrate to connect services your app should read from, write to, or trigger. Common integrations include Google Sheets, Airtable, Slack, OpenAI, Email, Notion, Microsoft Teams, and any other integration available in your workspace.
5
Choose Plan first or build now
Use Plan first when the request is new, broad, or connected to multiple pages, roles, approvals, dashboards, database changes, or integrations. Build directly when your first request is small and specific. Building from the home page prompt starts in Auto, unless you chose Plan first. Learn more in Agent Modes.
6
Submit a specific prompt
Include the app type, users, workflow, important views, and any login requirements. The more concrete your first prompt is, the better Zite can plan and build the first version.

Choose the right mode

Agent Modes
Agent Modes
Copy page

Learn how Zite’s Auto, Build, Plan, and Chat modes help you plan, create, and ask questions.

Zite’s agent modes control what kind of work the agent does. Use them to decide whether Zite should keep building with fewer approval stops, ask before certain changes, plan first, or answer questions without changing your project.
Auto is the default on the home page and in the app editor. Switch to Build when you want a checkpoint before certain changes. If you prefer Build, choose it from the mode menu and Zite will remember it for that workspace.
​
Choose the right mode
Mode	Best for	Makes changes?
Auto mode	Hands-free building with fewer approval stops	Yes
Build mode	Creating, updating, or fixing your app, with a checkpoint before certain changes	Yes
Plan mode	Scoping and clarifying requirements before building	No, it creates a plan
Chat mode	Asking questions or getting suggestions	No
Auto keeps building like Build but skips most Approve clicks. It still stops for logins, secrets, new apps, and questions — and it isn’t a true leave-and-forget background agent.
For large projects or unclear requirements, start in Plan mode. It helps clarify scope before Zite makes changes.
​
Switching modes
On the Zite app editor, open the mode menu on the lower left and choose the mode you want. You can also press Shift + Tab or Cmd/Ctrl + . on your keyboard.
The same mode control is available on the workspace home.

How to Build
Design tools
Copy page

Make your website, app, or internal tool feel clear, cohesive, and on-brand.

​
Overview
Good design in Zite starts with a system, not a collection of one-off tweaks. Choose the overall style first, then refine individual sections once the app has a consistent foundation.
If you already have company colors, fonts, a logo, or brand rules, start with a Brand Kit. If you only need a small text, color, spacing, or layout change, use Selective Edits.
​
Start with the whole design
New builders often start by fixing the first thing that looks wrong: one button, one card, one heading, one color. That can work for small issues, but it can also make the app feel patched together.
Before editing individual components, decide the app’s design direction:
What you have	Best starting point
A real company brand	Create or apply a Brand Kit.
A website you want to match	Paste the website link in chat and say what to use as reference.
A screenshot or mockup	Upload it with + followed by Upload an attachment.
A page needs images	Ask Zite to create placeholder, illustration, or marketing visuals.
No brand yet	Choose a theme, then refine colors, typography, and spacing.
Design systems work because the same decisions repeat: the same font scale, button style, color roles, card treatment, spacing rhythm, and navigation patterns. In Zite, global theme and Brand Kit changes are the fastest way to create that consistency.
​
Use Brand Kit or themes for global style
Use global design controls when the change should apply across the app. This keeps the app easier to maintain and prevents each page from drifting into a different visual style.
Use a Brand Kit when you want Zite to reuse a brand across multiple apps. Brand Kits can include logos, icons, fonts, color palettes, button styles, card styles, and written guidelines.
Use a theme when you want to quickly set the look of one app. Click the  swatch icon, then choose the theme or Brand Kit you want to apply.
Global changes are best for:
Main fonts and type scale
Primary, secondary, accent, background, and text colors
Button shape, color, and weight
Card, panel, and table styling
Overall spacing and density
Light or dark visual direction
Navigation and page-level layout patterns
Applying a theme from the design panel does not use credits. AI-powered design work, such as changing a design from an uploaded photo, does use credits.
​
Set fonts and colors
Fonts and colors should usually be configured in your theme or Brand Kit first. That keeps headings, body text, buttons, backgrounds, cards, and links consistent across the app.
Use individual edits when a specific section needs a local adjustment, such as making one heading larger, changing a single button color

How to Build
Create a brand kit
Copy page

Keep your branding consistent by using the same colors, fonts, icons, and logo across your Zite apps.

​
Overview
Building multiple apps and landing pages for the same company or brand requires staying within brand guidelines to ensure a consistent look and feel across everything you create. Without a shared system, it can be difficult to keep colors, fonts, and styling aligned across different projects.
A brand kit helps solve this by keeping your key brand elements in one place so you can easily apply them across all apps and pages.
Brand kits are applied per app, not per workspace. Apps in the same workspace can use the same brand kit or different ones, but you must select and apply the desired brand kit separately in each app.
Free, Pro, and Business organizations can have one brand kit. Team and Enterprise plans include unlimited brand kits.
​
What is a brand kit?
It’s a centralized hub containing the visual styling elements that represent your brand. It contains the following:
Logo: The primary visual symbol used in app headers and nav bars
Icon: A small square logo used as favicon and app icon
Font: The main text style
Color Palette: Primary and secondary colors, including accents if any
Guidelines: A set of rules that define how a brand should look and be presented
​
Build your brand kit
1

Choose how to set up

You can create or access a brand kit in three places:
In the initial app prompt box, click the swatch icon  and select Create brand kit.
In the app editor, click the swatch icon , then open Theme.
From Settings, open Brand kit.
In the popup, you can either Import your website or Create manually. For our example, let’s use Zite’s website.
You can change the logo or icon by clicking x and uploading or dropping a file.
2

Add or edit your brand assets

Importing will automatically capture a website’s brand information and styling.
This is includes the logos, color palette, font, button, and card styles. You are free to edit these however you see fit.
3

Review guidelines

Importing also captures brand guidelines, specifically Visual Style, Tone of Voice, and Business Context. You can add more to this or edit them as needed.
Click Create Brand Kit once you’ve reviewed all the details.
That’s it! You’ll now see your brand kit when creating an app.
​
Keep colors readable
When Zite creates a theme from your brand kit, it checks the contrast between text and backgrounds. It adjusts text, chart colors, and focus indicators where needed while keeping your main brand colors for backgrounds and buttons.
Review the result in your app, especially if you’ve made individual color changes. For a wider check of readability and keyboard use, ask the Accessibility agent to review it.
​
Edit an existing brand kit
On the dashboard, click your Account name followed by Settings.
Navigate to Branding kit and click your brand to edit it.

How to Build
Zite Workflows
Copy page

Add backend logic to your Zite apps—connect to databases, send emails, run AI, and more.

​
What are workflows?
Workflows are the backend logic that powers your Zite apps. They let you:
Connect to databases: Read and write data from Zite Database, Airtable, Google Sheets, and more
Send messages: Trigger Slack notifications or send emails
Run AI operations: Generate text, images, or structured data with OpenAI
Process data: Transform, filter, and combine data from multiple sources
Call external APIs: Connect to third-party services
Workflows are sometimes called endpoints or API routes.
​
Create workflows
1

Describe the logic

Tell Zite what you want the workflow to do. For example:
Create a workflow that searches for products by name 
and returns matching results with their prices.

2

Connect integrations

If the workflow needs access to a service (like Slack or Airtable), Zite will prompt you to + Connect it.
3

Review and test

Zite generates the workflow and shows you a visual preview of what it does. Use Test run to verify it works as expected. More info here.
For authenticated workflows, choose which user context to test with
Be specific in your prompts. Instead of “save user data,” try “when a user submits the form, create a new record in the Contacts table with their name and email.”
​
Available integrations
Workflows can connect to all Zite integrations.
Browse integrations at zite.com/integrations.
Learn how to link your accounts and use integrations in your app here.
​
View workflows
Click Workflows see all workflows in your app. Each workflow shows a name, its description, apps it uses (Database, Slack, OpenAI, etc.), and who has access.
Click any workflow to open the editor, where you can view the code, see a visual preview, or check the run history.
Name - The workflow’s identifier
Description - What the workflow does
Integration icons - Which services the workflow uses
​
Authentication
Workflows can require users to be logged in. When authentication is enabled:
Only logged-in users can trigger the workflow
The workflow has access to the current user’s info (ID, email, profile data)
Requests from non-logged-in users are automatically rejected
Authentication
Set up authentication for your app.
​
Workflow editor
The workflow editor has three tabs:
Tab	Description
Preview	Visual diagram showing the workflow’s steps
Code	The TypeScript code powering the workflow
History	Execution logs for debugging (learn more)
You don’t need to write or understand code to use Zite Workflows. The code tab is there if you want to inspect or manually edit the logic.
​
Streaming workflows
For real-time AI chat experiences, workflows can stream responses back to the user as they’re generated, just like ChatGPT.
Ask Zite to “create a chat interface” or “add an AI assistant,” and it will set up a streaming workflow

Code viewing & editing
Copy page

View, edit, download, run, and review the code for your Zite project.

Zite projects use a monorepo: one codebase contains every app in the workspace, along with shared packages and project configuration. When you add an app to an existing workspace, Zite adds it to the same monorepo instead of creating a separate codebase.
Code view lets you browse the entire project, edit supported files, create files, run the workspace locally, and review the history of code changes.
Direct code editing is intended for seasoned developers. For most changes, work with the Zite agent so it can update related files and keep the project consistent.
​
Open code view
Open a project.
Click the project or app name in the top-left corner.
Under Workspace, select Code.
The file tree appears on the left. Select a file to open it in the editor, use the search field to find a file by name, or expand folders to explore the project.
​
Understand the monorepo
All apps in a workspace are bundled into the same project codebase. The file tree commonly includes:
Path	What it contains
apps/<app-name>	The source code and configuration for an individual app. Each additional app gets its own folder here.
packages/<package-name>	Components or other code shared by apps in the workspace.
Project root	Workspace-level packages, TypeScript configuration, Zite configuration, and other shared files.
Before changing a shared package, check which apps use it. A shared-code change can affect more than one app.
​
View and edit code
Click a file in the tree to open it, then edit the code directly. Files with a lock icon are managed by Zite and cannot be edited from Code view.
Direct edits are most useful when you know which file needs to change and are comfortable with React, TypeScript, and the project structure. For changes that cross multiple files or apps, ask the Zite agent to make the update instead.
To add a file, click the new-file icon beside the search field, then enter its name and extension. Follow the conventions already used in that app or package.
If you are unsure what a file does, use Explain file with AI before editing it. Zite opens Chat mode with the selected file as context, so you can ask follow-up questions without changing the project.
​
Review code history
Zite keeps a Git-backed history of meaningful project changes. Use it to connect code updates to prompts or agent actions and see exactly which files changed.
Click History in the Code view toolbar.
Select a change from the timeline.
Choose Code to see the files changed and a side-by-side diff.
Use the project selector to review changes across the entire project or within an individual app.
To return the project to an earlier working state, see Restore an older version.
​
Best practices
Use the Zite agent for changes that affect multiple files, apps, or shared packages.
Check whether code under packages is used by other apps before editing it.

Zite Database
Copy page

Zite Database is an agent-ready database built to power multiple apps from one shared source of truth. Create, manage, and scale your data with agents in Zite or through MCP.

Use the built-in Database Agent to create tables, organize data, analyze records, and make updates directly in Zite.
You can also connect external AI tools through Zite MCP, giving agents secure read and write access to your databases. Collaborate with your whole team without seat limits, and scale to millions of records as your apps grow.
​
What’s included
Database Agent - Build tables, organize data, analyze records, and make updates with an agent inside Zite
MCP access - Let AI tools securely query and maintain your databases through Zite MCP
AI fields - Automatically categorize, summarize, score, and enrich every record
20+ field types - Text, numbers, dates, files, linked records, and more
Airtable migration - Move your existing Airtable bases to Zite
Data import/export - Import data from Airtable, Google Sheets, or CSV, and export it for analysis
REST API + Webhooks - Programmatic access with up to 30 API requests per second, per database
Linked records - Create relationships between tables
Bulk operations - Update or delete multiple records at once
Granular permissions - Control who can view or edit your data
Undo/redo - Easily revert changes
Multiple views - Organize and filter your data
​
Performance
Zite Database is built for speed:
50 internal Zite Database requests per second - Support non-API activity, per database
Millions of records - Scale your database as your app grows
Fast queries - Get results instantly, even with complex filters
​
Managing your database
Access the full database interface:
Add or remove fields
Create new tables
Migrate existing Airtable bases
Import data from Airtable, Google Sheets, or CSV
Add AI fields that generate and maintain values automatically
Bulk edit records
Set up webhooks
Use the REST API
Once a database has 8 or more tables, a button at the start of the table tabs opens a searchable list of all tables.
​
Pricing
Zite Database includes unlimited seats on every plan, including the free tier. There are fixed pricing tiers based on data storage, view pricing here.
​
